newsitem.title: UK: Conservatives, Labour trade jibes in UK campaign.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives, Labour trade jibes in UK campaign.

text.p: The ruling Conservatives and their Labour rivals, who polls tip to win Britain's May 1 election, traded accusations of sleaze and "gutter" tactics on Sunday as the campaign turned bitter.
But as Prime Minister John Major and Labour leader Tony Blair slugged it out, a new poll showed voters were unaffected by the start of Britain's longest election campaign in 80 years.

The first opinion poll carried out since Major announced the election last Monday showed that support for the parties had barely changed since the beginning of the month despite an increasingly hard-fought campaign.
The Gallup poll for The Sunday Telegraph newspaper showed Labour's lead remained a huge 25.5 points -- enough to give the party a landslide majority after 18 years out of power.
The Labour leader, bidding to become the country's youngest prime minister this century, only needs a 4.3 percent swing from the 1992 election for an overall parliamentary majority.

Blair, 43, has dragged Labour from the left to the centre to make it electable since becoming leader in 1994. But on Sunday, he showed he was aware of the risks he faces, saying his party would be finished if it broke its new pledges to voters.

"If I break my promises on tax, on not raising basic and top rate tax, on trade unions and these essential things that I have said we will do, we are gone. We are probably finished forever," Blair said in an interview for the News of the World.
Labour has ditched historic commitments over the public ownership of major industries and has pledged not to raise income tax rates for the first five years after winning power.
But Major, battling against a growing scandal over sleaze enveloping 10 ruling party members of parliament, lashed out at the "fancy face" of new Labour.
"They are presenting, in my judgement, a completely false face to the public," Major told the News of the World.
The growing bitterness between the two main parties was plain in Sunday morning television interviews with top figures from the Conservative and Labour campaign teams.

Peter Mandelson, head of Labour's campaign team, renewed the attack on sleaze, challenging Major to recall parliament to hear a report by a parliamentary ethics watchdog into the allegations of influence peddling by the 10 Conservative MPs.

Major's decision to announce the election last week and close parliament on Monday means a report into the allegations cannnot be published before the election unless the government, in an extraordinary climb-down, recalls the House of Commons.
"If he refuses to recall parliament, then that must carry the implication that he's trying to cover up the truth," Mandelson told a BBC interviewer.
But Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine accused Labour on the same programme of trying to stir up the sleaze scandal to distract attention from excellent economic statistics.

Adding that the report could not be published before May 1 without denying those affected the chance to properly defend themselves, he accused Labour of stooping to "gutter levels of opportunistic campaigning".
"It is a total travesty of the truth...," said Heseltine.
"Tony Blair is conducting perhaps the most professionally phony campaign this country has ever seen."
